Linus Tech Tips:
16.8 million subscribers,
one controversy, and what
we can all learn from it.

LTT is one of the most influential tech channels ever built — 9.4 billion views, a genuine product business, and a community that shaped how a generation thinks about hardware. In 2023 a very public controversy tested all of it. Here is what happened, what was fair, and what the tech community should take from it.

Jarrit Hosking
Forge Vertical · Cape Town · September 2, 2026
12 min read
// What Linus Tech Tips actually built

Before the controversy, before the criticism, before any of 2023 — let's start with what Linus Sebastian actually built, because it is genuinely remarkable.

Linus Gabriel Sebastian started his channel in 2008 while working as a presenter for Canadian computer retailer NCIX. In October 2012 he founded Linus Media Group, formally launching it in 2013. By 2026 the main Linus Tech Tips channel has 16.8 million subscribers and 9.44 billion views. That is not a YouTube channel. That is a media institution.

The LTT ecosystem extends well beyond a single channel. There is the main LTT channel, ShortCircuit, TechLinked, Techquickie, Mac Address, and the WAN Show — a weekly podcast that runs long and unscripted. There is Floatplane, an independent streaming platform. And there is LTTStore.com — not merch as an afterthought, but a genuine product business. The LTT Store sells screwdrivers, backpacks, magnetic cable management systems, desk pads, and apparel — products described as "engineered, not merch" and "built like someone will take it apart."

The screwdriver became something of a legend in the tech community. It is overbuilt, magnetic, well-reviewed by the community, and genuinely useful. That is the standard Linus set for himself: things that work, made for people who care how things work.

What happened in 2023 — the full honest account

// Chapter 01 — Billet Labs, Gamers Nexus, and the fallout

In August 2023, Gamers Nexus — a competing tech YouTube channel run by Steve Burke — published a nearly 45-minute video titled "The Problem with Linus Tech Tips: Accuracy, Ethics and Responsibility."

The criticisms were specific and documented. Burke and Gamers Nexus accused LTT of significant and frequent data errors, rushing content out the door in pursuit of quantity over quality, and using disclaimers that were so brief that viewers would rarely see them.

The centrepiece of the criticism was a small company called Billet Labs. In June 2023, Linus posted a video about a copper cooler prototype developed by Billet Labs. According to Gamers Nexus, Linus failed to use the device according to the correct specifications, instead deciding the product was useless. Gamers Nexus also noted that LTT auctioned off the loaned one-of-a-kind prototype against the wishes of Billet Labs — a prototype that had cost several thousand dollars to produce.

LTT responded that the prototype was "auctioned for charity due to a miscommunication" rather than sold. Gamers Nexus argued in a follow-up that the response was inaccurate. Billet Labs paid tribute to Burke's integrity while making clear they held LTT in lesser regard — noting that "there was no apology" in the initial email they received about the device.

LTT halted production for a week. The broader takeaway from the Gamers Nexus video was that Linus Tech Tips was cutting corners to maintain its publishing pace — and getting defensive when called out rather than correcting the record.

For the most part, the core scandal died down after the hiatus. Linus stepped back from the CEO role — he had actually stepped down in June 2023 before the controversy broke — transitioning to Chief Vision Officer to focus on long-term strategy. The channel continued. The community largely stayed.

This is what happens when scale outpaces systems. LTT was publishing near-daily across multiple channels. At that pace, something was always going to break. The question is not whether mistakes happen — it is what you do when they do.

What was fair criticism and what was not

// Chapter 02 — An honest read

The Billet Labs situation was genuinely wrong. A small company loaned a one-of-a-kind prototype to a massive channel. The review was careless. The prototype was disposed of without consent. There was no adequate apology. That part of the criticism was fair and the harm was real — to a small company that had taken a significant risk to get their product in front of an audience.

The broader "quantity over quality" criticism is harder to evaluate. LTT publishes across multiple channels at a pace that almost no other tech operation matches. At that volume, some errors are statistically inevitable. The question is whether errors are corrected transparently or buried — and the 2023 response suggested the latter. That needed to change and largely did.

The Gamers Nexus vs LTT tension continued into 2025 with additional plagiarism allegations, which LTT called "false and damaging." Linus responded on the WAN Show saying he wanted to stop the situation from dragging out. At some point, long-running public feuds between creators stop being about accountability and start being about something else. The original criticism was legitimate. Extended conflict for its own sake rarely serves anyone — least of all the audience.

The Billet Labs lesson for anyone building in public: When you have scale, you have power. A positive review from LTT can make a small company. A careless or negative one can break it. That asymmetry comes with responsibility — particularly when you are handling someone's prototype, which represents their investment, their IP, and sometimes their entire bet on a product.

What the tech community should take from this

// Chapter 03 — A different kind of accountability

The tech content ecosystem has a problem with criticism as performance. The 45-minute callout video format — detailed, evidence-backed, devastating — has become its own genre. It is sometimes necessary. It is sometimes disproportionate. The line between accountability and entertainment at another creator's expense is not always clearly drawn.

Good criticism guides. It identifies a specific failure, explains why it is a failure, and gives the person a path to do better. Spirit-breaking criticism — the kind designed to maximise damage rather than produce change — serves the audience of the critic more than it serves the person being criticised or the community they share.

Linus Sebastian has spent 18 years building something genuinely useful. He was wrong about Billet Labs. He handled it badly initially. He has also made it easier for millions of people to understand hardware, make better purchasing decisions, and feel like technology is something they can understand rather than fear. Both things are true.

The tech community is stronger when it operates on the principle of supporting what deserves support and correcting what needs correcting — without the correction becoming the point. If you see a creator doing something right, say so. If you see something wrong, say that too. But ask yourself whether the goal is improvement or impact.

From Cape Town to wherever you are building: This is a site built by one person in South Africa who finds Linus, NetworkChuck, and Chris Titus Tech genuinely inspiring — not because they are perfect but because they showed up, built something real, and kept going. That is the standard. Build something useful. Keep it honest. Fix it when it breaks. That is the whole game.

Where LTT stands in 2026

// Chapter 04 — Still going strong

Linus Tech Tips describes itself as a passionate team of "professionally curious" experts in consumer technology and video production who aim to educate and entertain. That description still fits. The channel is still publishing. The store is still shipping. The LTT Store recently launched UV-reactive ratcheting screwdrivers and a new magnetic cable management system — products designed by people who genuinely care about the tools they use.

Linus Sebastian transitioned from CEO to Chief Vision Officer in 2023, stepping back from day-to-day operations to focus on long-term creative strategy. That is not a retreat. It is someone recognising that the thing they built needs different management than the thing they started — and having the self-awareness to make that call.

The 9.44 billion views did not come from perfect execution. They came from 18 years of showing up, caring about hardware, and making technology accessible to people who wanted to understand it. That record is real regardless of 2023.
